question: A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 3-minute episode of a tonic-clonic seizure. The parents deny any previous history of seizure involving the patient or the family. Physical examination reveals an afebrile, well-groomed, and playful appearance, with normal vital signs. The patient carries a pink birthmark on the right side of her face extending from the forehead to the zygomatic arch. Which of the following findings is most likely on a head CT of this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Tonic-clonic seizure" -> "No family history of seizures" -> "Pink birthmark on face" -> "Sturge-Weber syndrome consideration" -> "Prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Tonic-clonic seizure" -> "Pink birthmark on face" -> "Sturge-Weber syndrome suspicion" -> "Prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Tonic-clonic seizure" -> "No fever" -> "Pink birthmark on face" -> "Sturge-Weber syndrome" -> "Prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Tonic-clonic seizure" -> "Pink birthmark on face" -> "Sturge-Weber syndrome" -> "Possible calcification" -> "Prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification" -> 75%
analysis: The clinical presentation of a 2-year-old girl with a facial birthmark resembling a port-wine stain suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome. This condition is characterized by a facial capillary malformation (port-wine stain) and neurological abnormalities, including seizures. A common finding on head CT in Sturge-Weber syndrome is intracranial calcifications, often described as 'tram-track' calcifications, which are prominent in the cortical and subcortical regions. Therefore, the most likely finding on a head CT for this patient is prominent intraparenchymal white matter calcification.
